title: Why History Matters
author: Elizabeth Stice
summary: Stice reviews David McCullough's posthumous collection History Matters to argue for history's place in education and its role in forming character. McCullough held that history serves two purposes: it gives perspective on one's own brief life and it builds character by proxying readers toward examples of courage and discipline. He chose to write about admirable figures (Washington, Adams, Truman) not hagiographically but with full humanity and flaw, believing that understanding people in their own era and respecting genuine character transcends nostalgia. The piece defends history against charges of irrelevance, arguing that the discipline offers something no amount of contemporary skill training can replace: the patient work of understanding what courage and character actually look like in practice.
points: History gives proportion and context: It shows how brief one's own life is and puts contemporary anxieties in longer view.
Character is the decisive quality: McCullough believed character mattered more in public life than policy expertise, and history teaches character through example.
Accuracy and humanity go together: Real history means acknowledging flaws and understanding people in their own era, not hagiography or nostalgia.
Schools are losing historical literacy: McCullough voiced concern about young people's ignorance of history; Stice echoes this as a curricular crisis.
Patient discipline of understanding: The work of history is slow and meticulous, the opposite of modern speed; it teaches a valuable epistemological habit.
quotes: David McCullough had a very distinctive voice. He was an English major who became perhaps America's most popular history writer, capable of crafting compelling narrative from years of meticulous research. He was thoroughly patriotic but wrote about the people of the past as people, not marble ideals.

The chapters in this book present compelling arguments for the importance of history and character and they help us see a bit more of the man behind the famous voice.” “I'm convinced that history encourages, as nothing else does, a sense of proportion about life, gives us a sense of the relative scale of our own brief time on earth and how valuable that is.

This book is a cri de coeur for a discipline too often neglected by undergraduates. The rise in historical illiteracy was very concerning to McCullough and this concern appears on a number of these pages.

Again and again, we see the importance of character for McCullough. It was not only seemingly one of his criteria for writing a biography, but it is perhaps the chief lesson he hopes we will draw from history.
character counts in the presidency more than any other single quality. It is more important than how much the president knows of foreign policy or economics, or even about politics.

He emphasizes the importance of being familiar with what the people of another time were reading. In many of the letters exchanged by John and Abigail Adams, plays and books are referenced, without quotation marks. Those passages show us the world these people inhabited and also the peril that awaits later generations who attempt to interpret these letters but fail to appreciate context.

His own story is like that of many of his subjects, talent married to hard work. It includes the trappings of a certain kind of life, with a typewriter and a writing cabin and a patient wife. But he did not live in a simpler time, he crafted his life in our time.

His life and books were not built on nostalgia but decades of research and endless revisions. He had a very pleasing baritone, but his voice will persist because of its emphasis on courage and character and appreciation of the past.” Archived from Mere Orthodoxy on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
